analysis.one_liner: Exempts certain commissioned sales employees from federal minimum wage and overtime rules.
analysis.headline: The bill never left the Senate Labor and Human Resources Committee and died when the 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999, without any vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend the Fair Labor Standards Act — the law requiring employers to pay at least the minimum wage and time-and-a-half for overtime — so that it no longer applies to certain sales employees. It would cover workers in sales jobs that require specialized knowledge of the product, focus on existing customers or repeat sales, and are paid a base salary plus a commission on each sale. If enacted, those employees could be required to work long hours with no extra pay and could fall below the minimum wage on an hourly basis. The bill was introduced by Sen. Paul Coverdell in June 1998, referred to the Labor and Human Resources Committee, and never received a hearing, a vote, or floor action before Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Employers who rely heavily on commissioned sales staff — such as software, telecommunications, and direct-sales companies — would gain because they could base pay entirely on sales output without any overtime obligation, cutting payroll costs and giving managers more flexibility over long hours.

how_it_helps.text: The bill would exempt sales employees who earn at least 1.5 times the minimum wage times 2,080 hours in base pay (about $15,080 at the 1998 minimum wage) plus sales-based compensation of at least 40 percent of that same amount, removing them from minimum wage, recordkeeping, and overtime requirements. [S2] [S3]

Employers argue the existing overtime rules fit poorly with commissioned sales work, where pay is tied to output rather than hours, and that the exemption would let companies reward top performers more flexibly. [S2] [S3]

analysis.who_pays: If the bill passed, the covered sales employees would bear the cost: they could work unlimited hours with no overtime premium, and if a slow period drove hourly-equivalent pay below the minimum wage, the law would no longer require the employer to make up the difference. Recordkeeping requirements would also disappear, making it harder to verify pay.

drawbacks.text: Removing overtime and minimum wage protection means employees who are classified into this exempt category could see their effective hourly pay fall during slow sales periods and could be required to work long hours at no extra compensation. [S3]
The exemption would eliminate recordkeeping requirements for these employees, which are the practical means by which wage-and-hour violations are detected and proven. [S2] [S3]

A supporter would counter that the thresholds are restrictive — the employee must earn substantial base pay plus sizable commissions — and that the exemption targets well-compensated professionals rather than low-wage workers, so the practical risk of abuse is limited. [S2] [S3]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill is a fairly narrow carve-out rather than a sweeping change: its eligibility thresholds are set high enough to reach only a subset of sales jobs, and supporters argued those workers are commission professionals the Depression-era wage law was never designed for. But for the workers it covers, the trade is one-sided — the employer gains flexibility and lower costs, while the employee loses the only federal guarantee of a minimum hourly floor and overtime pay. For ordinary people overall, the costs outweigh the gains.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Labor and Human Resources Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never acted on it, so it died when the 105th Congress ended in January 1999.

narrative.text: Sen. Paul Coverdell introduced the bill on June 9, 1998, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Labor and Human Resources. [S1] [S5]
One Republican senator cosponsored the bill. [S4]
The committee took no further action — no hearing, markup, or floor vote appears in the record — and the bill expired when the 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999. [S5]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Commissioned sales employees kept their federal minimum wage and overtime protections, since no exemption was enacted. Employers gained nothing from this bill's death beyond avoiding the change they had sought.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Covered sales workers kept wage protections

for.what_they_did: Pressed Congress for an exemption from overtime rules for commissioned sales employees, a campaign that produced this bill and parallel House legislation in the late 1990s.

against.name: Senate Committee on Labor and Human Resources

against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on June 9, 1998, and took no further action; the bill never reached a hearing, a markup, or the Senate floor.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken. The sponsor and its single cosponsor were both Republicans, and the bill died in committee without opposition ever having to declare itself.

industries.industry: Employers of commissioned inside sales staff (software, telecommunications, direct-sales)
industries.note: The bill would have freed these employers from minimum wage, recordkeeping, and overtime obligations for eligible sales staff, letting pay ride entirely on commissions. The employer's gain comes directly out of the covered workers' pay protections.
Covered workers would have lost overtime pay, the hourly minimum wage floor, and the payroll records used to enforce both. Their interest ran directly against the bill.
